content: 1. Transient increases in plasma HIV-RNA load have been observed following the administration of several vaccines. However, current evidence suggests that these increases are not clinically significant. 2. Infants, children, and adolescents exposed to or living with HIV should receive all vaccines recommended under national immunization schedules. 3. COVID-19 vaccine trials have included a limited number of people living with HIV. Despite the limited data, WHO-recommended COVID-19 vaccines are considered safe for individuals with HIV. No interactions have been reported between COVID-19 vaccines and antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, which should be continued after vaccination to maintain health. 4. Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination is recommended for people living with HIV, including children, if they are on antiretroviral therapy (ART), clinically well, and immunologically stable (CD4% > 25% for children under five years old). Neonates born to women of unknown HIV status should also be vaccinated, as the benefits outweigh the risks. For neonates confirmed to have HIV, BCG vaccination should be delayed until ART is initiated and immunological stability is achieved. 5. A systematic review in 2014 found that higher doses of the hepatitis B vaccine resulted in higher peak anti-HBs antibody titers in adults living with HIV compared to standard doses. However, there was no significant difference in the proportion of adults with protective antibodies up to five years post-vaccination. 6. Tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines are suitable for immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV, though their immune response may be lower than in fully immunocompetent individuals. All children living with HIV should be vaccinated against tetanus according to general population recommendations. 7. Measles vaccination should be routinely administered to asymptomatic children and adults living with HIV. In areas with high HIV and measles incidence, an initial dose may be given as early as six months of age, followed by routine doses per national schedules. A supplementary dose is recommended for HIV-infected or exposed infants from six months of age. 8. Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines should be introduced as part of a strategy to prevent cervical cancer, targeting girls aged 9–14 years before sexual activity. A three-dose schedule is recommended for those older than 15 years or immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV, regardless of ART status. Screening for HPV or HIV infection before vaccination is unnecessary. 9. Cholera vaccination should be part of comprehensive cholera control strategies, especially in humanitarian emergencies with a risk of cholera. Pregnant and lactating women and people living with HIV should be included in oral cholera vaccine campaigns due to high potential benefits and minimal risks. 10. There is no safety data for the dengue vaccine CYD-TDV in individuals with immunodeficiency or HIV. The manufacturer advises against its use in symptomatic HIV infection or asymptomatic HIV with evidence of impaired immune function. 11. Infants living with HIV and preterm neonates who received three primary doses of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines before 12 months of age may benefit from a booster dose in their second year of life. 12. Rubella-containing vaccines should not be administered to individuals with severe immunodeficiency, including those with symptomatic HIV infection or AIDS. 13. While the typhoid Vi-polysaccharide vaccine is safe for people living with HIV, its effectiveness depends on CD4 cell count. The oral typhoid vaccine Ty21a can be given to immunologically stable individuals with HIV but is not recommended for those with impaired cell-mediated immunity. 14. Skin and oral conditions are highly prevalent among people living with HIV, especially with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³. These conditions can cause significant morbidity, stigma, and reduced quality of life. ART is the primary treatment for many of these conditions, such as Kaposi’s sarcoma and eosinophilic folliculitis. 15. Nutritional care is critical for people living with HIV, as the infection increases energy demands and can lead to weight loss and wasting. Nutritional assessment and support should be integrated into HIV care, with food supplements provided in food-insecure contexts to support recovery. 16. For infants and young children living with HIV, optimal feeding practices, including exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and continued breastfeeding with complementary feeding for at least 24 months, are essential. Growth monitoring should be part of ART response assessment, and poor growth should prompt further evaluation and intervention.
